title: The Second Night: All Problems Are Interpersonal Relationship Problems
coreMove: Notice when another person's movement has been converted into your rank, then return attention to the task instead of the scoreboard.
sourcePressure: The source supports the second night as the rivalry chapter: inferiority as subjective assumption, bragging as linked to inferiority, life not as competition, escalation into power struggle and revenge, and life tasks as the exit.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says stop comparing yourself and build self-esteem; the real move exposes the rank logic that turns other people into threats and tasks into scoreboards.

sourceAnchors.name: Feelings of Inferiority Are Subjective Assumptions
sourceAnchors.detail: The frozen source lists this as a visible heading in the second night.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The promotion did not shrink you; the rank story you attached to it did.

sourceAnchors.name: From Power Struggle to Revenge
sourceAnchors.detail: The frozen source lists this heading in the second night, supporting an escalation from competition into retaliation.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A scoreboard does not stay harmless for long; when pride loses, it starts looking for a way to collect.

hook: Comparison is the thief of joy
Someone else's success is not your failure
counterintuition: Inferiority is all in your head
tryThisNow: Unfollow someone who makes you feel bad
examples: promotion jealousy in a generic office

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.audience: a project architect who turns a peer's promotion into proof that her own portfolio is worthless
exampleSpecs.stakes: the museum proposal needs clear judgment, but the rank story is making every design review feel like a trial
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sophie draws a line down her notebook separating the actual proposal revision from the private rank verdict she added when the promotion was announced.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Graphite dust smears across the corner of a museum elevation.

exampleSpecs.audience: a recreational runner whose training collapses whenever a clubmate posts a faster split
exampleSpecs.stakes: a spring marathon plan is turning into punishment instead of preparation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 6:18 a.m., Lukas erases his planned easy pace after seeing the club board, then has to restore it because the task is recovery, not beating the name above his.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 6:18 a.m., Lukas stands in front of the laminated pace board with a wet glove in one hand.

exampleSpecs.audience: a postdoctoral researcher who brags about methods knowledge whenever another lab member gets credit
exampleSpecs.stakes: a collaboration may fracture before a grant resubmission if superiority theater keeps replacing shared work
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Claire hears herself naming every technique she knows, then stops and asks what the grant revision actually needs from her instead of what status she wants restored.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "I ran that assay before anyone here knew the protocol," Claire says, and the pipette box clicks shut.

exampleSpecs.audience: a bookseller who quietly wants a neighboring shop to fail after it wins a local prize
exampleSpecs.stakes: a joint literacy festival will collapse if rivalry turns into strategic withholding
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ben catches the satisfaction he feels when the rival shop's shipment is delayed and names it as revenge rather than business realism.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What do you call the small pleasure when the other shop's boxes do not arrive?

exampleSpecs.audience: a producer who lets donor numbers turn colleagues into enemies during a campaign week
exampleSpecs.stakes: the final drive segment needs cooperation, but leaderboard rank has made every script note feel like humiliation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ingrid covers the leaderboard with the rundown sheet and asks what the next hour of radio requires if nobody's donor total counts as a verdict.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The studio light is still red, and the donor leaderboard glows behind the glass.

exampleSpecs.audience: an amateur singer who treats another tenor's solo as public demotion
exampleSpecs.stakes: a memorial performance risks becoming a private status wound rather than a shared act of care
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Yusuf move from rehearsing revenge in his head to marking the exact entrances he owes the choir behind the soloist.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You see the pencil stop over the word 'solo' in the choral score.

skillTargets: identify the status interpretation added to a neutral event
distinguish real task seriousness from rank hunger
spot superiority display as dependence on audience rather than confidence
analyze when power struggle has hardened into revenge

tryThisNowSpec: Choose one comparison from today and write two columns: what actually happened, and the rank verdict you added to it.
